name: english_set6_p1
label: English Language: set 6 (comprehension approach, essays, letters, speeches, reports and articles)

papers.title: Approaching a Comprehension Passage: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on approaching a comprehension passage, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: *What does the writer mean by "the city never sleeps"?* This is
questions.explanation:
A figurative question asks you to explain an image or expression in plain words: here, that the city is busy and active day and night.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a literal question: A literal question asks for a fact stated in the passage, such as *What…? Where…? When…?*
- a grammatical question: A grammatical question asks for the name and function of a phrase or clause.
- a vocabulary question: A vocabulary question asks for a word that could replace one in the passage.

options.label: A
options.content: a figurative question

options.label: B
options.content: a literal question

options.label: C
options.content: a grammatical question

options.label: D
options.content: a vocabulary question

questions.stem: Which is the best way to work through a comprehension test?
questions.explanation:
Reading in stages works: first for the big picture, then the questions, then a slow hunt for each answer, marking the lines in the margin.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Answer the questions first, then read the passage: Without reading the passage, the answers can only be guesses.
- Read only the first paragraph, then answer all the questions: Answers may come from any part of the passage.
- Read the questions and answer from general knowledge: Every answer must come from the passage, not from general knowledge.

options.label: A
options.content: Answer the questions first, then read the passage

options.label: B
options.content: Read the passage quickly for the main idea, read all the questions, then reread carefully to find each answer

options.label: C
options.content: Read only the first paragraph, then answer all the questions

options.label: D
options.content: Read the questions and answer from general knowledge

questions.stem: A question asks: *Why do you think the old man refused the money?* The passage never says why directly. The candidate should
questions.explanation:
This is an inferential question: the answer is suggested, not stated, so it must be built from details the passage gives.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- copy the sentence in which the money is mentioned: Copying the sentence does not give a reason; the question asks you to infer one.
- give a personal opinion with no link to the passage: Inferences must be supported by the passage, not invented.
- explain the meaning of the word *refused*: The question asks why, not what a word means.

options.label: A
options.content: copy the sentence in which the money is mentioned

options.label: B
options.content: give a personal opinion with no link to the passage

options.label: C
options.content: work out the reason from clues in the passage

options.label: D
options.content: explain the meaning of the word *refused*

questions.stem: In a vocabulary question (*find another word or phrase that could replace … as used in the passage*), the replacement must
questions.explanation:
Test your answer by putting it into the sentence: if it reads correctly and keeps the meaning, it is right. A noun must be replaced by a noun, a verb by a verb in the same form.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- be any word with a similar spelling: Spelling is irrelevant; meaning and word class are what matter.
- mean the opposite of the word in the passage: The replacement must mean the same, not the opposite.
- be a long explanation of the word: A replacement is a word or short phrase that could stand in the sentence.

options.label: A
options.content: be any word with a similar spelling

options.label: B
options.content: mean the opposite of the word in the passage

options.label: C
options.content: be a long explanation of the word

options.label: D
options.content: fit the sentence in the passage, with the same meaning and the same word class

questions.stem: A question asks for two reasons. A candidate writes down four. What is the risk?
questions.explanation:
Give exactly what is asked, clearly. Padding an answer with extra points wastes time and can lose marks.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- There is no risk: extra reasons always earn extra marks: Marks are given for the number of points asked, no more.
- The examiner will choose the best two of the four: Examiners are not required to search for the best points.
- The answer will be marked as a summary instead: It will still be marked as a comprehension answer.

options.label: A
options.content: The examiner may mark only the first two, and a wrong extra point can cost marks

options.label: B
options.content: There is no risk: extra reasons always earn extra marks

options.label: C
options.content: The examiner will choose the best two of the four

options.label: D
options.content: The answer will be marked as a summary instead

questions.stem: *How did the villagers cross the flooded river?* This question asks for
questions.explanation:
Read the question word twice: *why* needs a reason, *how* a manner or means, *what does … mean* an explanation.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the reason why they crossed: A reason answers *why*, not *how*.
- the time when they crossed: A time answers *when*.
- the place where they crossed: A place answers *where*.

options.label: A
options.content: the reason why they crossed

options.label: B
options.content: the way or means by which they crossed

options.label: C
options.content: the time when they crossed

options.label: D
options.content: the place where they crossed

questions.stem: Every answer in a comprehension test should be based on
questions.explanation:
Comprehension tests understanding of the given text. An answer that is true in real life but not in the passage scores nothing.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- what the candidate already knows about the topic: General knowledge can contradict the passage; the passage is the only source.
- the candidate's personal opinion: Opinions are not asked for unless the question says so, and even then they must relate to the passage.
- what other books say about the topic: Only the passage in front of you counts.

options.label: A
options.content: what the candidate already knows about the topic

options.label: B
options.content: the candidate's personal opinion

options.label: C
options.content: what the passage says or suggests

options.label: D
options.content: what other books say about the topic

papers.title: Essay Writing Fundamentals: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on essay writing fundamentals, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In the marking scheme for WASSCE essays taught in the lessons, which area carries the most marks?
questions.explanation:
Expression (precise vocabulary, varied sentences, suitable register, fluency) is worth twice as much as each of the other areas, and it improves steadily with practice.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Content (10 marks): Content carries 10 marks, half as many as expression.
- Organisation (10 marks): Organisation carries 10 marks.
- Mechanical accuracy (10 marks): Mechanical accuracy carries 10 marks.

options.label: A
options.content: Content (10 marks)

options.label: B
options.content: Organisation (10 marks)

options.label: C
options.content: Mechanical accuracy (10 marks)

options.label: D
options.content: Expression (20 marks)

questions.stem: A good paragraph in an essay usually
questions.explanation:
A paragraph is one idea, fully developed: usually four to seven sentences, explained and illustrated.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is a single sentence: One-sentence paragraphs lose organisation marks; an idea needs to be developed.
- covers every point of the essay at once: Several ideas crowded into one paragraph make the essay hard to follow.
- begins with *In conclusion*: *In conclusion* belongs only in the last paragraph, if at all.

options.label: A
options.content: develops one main idea, introduced by a topic sentence

options.label: B
options.content: is a single sentence

options.label: C
options.content: covers every point of the essay at once

options.label: D
options.content: begins with *In conclusion*

questions.stem: In the TEEL method of building a paragraph, the letters stand for
questions.explanation:
State the idea, explain how or why, make it concrete with an example, then link to the next idea or the question.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Title, Essay, Ending, Letter: These are not the parts of a paragraph.
- Topic, Evidence, Emotion, Language: Emotion and language are not steps of the method.
- Theme, Example, Explanation, List: A list is not part of the method, and the order is wrong.

options.label: A
options.content: Title, Essay, Ending, Letter

options.label: B
options.content: Topic sentence, Explanation, Example, Link

options.label: C
options.content: Topic, Evidence, Emotion, Language

options.label: D
options.content: Theme, Example, Explanation, List

questions.stem: A question asks for the causes of examination malpractice and the ways of stopping it. A candidate writes only about the causes. The essay will
questions.explanation:
Underline every part of the question before planning. *Causes and solutions*, *advantages and disadvantages*: both halves must be answered.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- score full marks, because the causes are well explained: However well the causes are explained, half the question is missing.
- lose only mechanical accuracy marks: Missing part of the question is a content fault, not a grammar fault.
- be marked as a different type of essay: It is marked against the question set, and the missing part costs marks.

options.label: A
options.content: score full marks, because the causes are well explained

options.label: B
options.content: lose only mechanical accuracy marks

options.label: C
options.content: lose content marks, because part of the question is not answered

options.label: D
options.content: be marked as a different type of essay

questions.stem: Which sentence shows the best expression for a WASSCE essay?
questions.explanation:
Good expression is precise and vivid: *crowded*, *shouting their prices*, *above the noise* let the reader see and hear the scene.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- In this contemporary dispensation of our socio-economic milieu, it is pertinent to note that the street was busy.  
  This is memorised 'big English': long words used without real meaning, which impresses no one.
- The street was very very busy and there was many people.  
  *Very very* is repetitive, and *there was many people* is a grammatical error.
- the street was busy wit traders: This has spelling, capital and punctuation errors.

options.label: A
options.content: In this contemporary dispensation of our socio-economic milieu, it is pertinent to note that the street was busy.

options.label: B
options.content: The street was very very busy and there was many people.

options.label: C
options.content: the street was busy wit traders

options.label: D
options.content: Traders crowded the narrow street, shouting their prices above the noise of the traffic.

questions.stem: Why should a candidate spend a few minutes planning before writing an essay?
questions.explanation:
A plan makes sure every part of the question is answered, ideas are not repeated, and each paragraph has one clear point.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- To copy out the question several times: Copying the question earns no marks.
- To write the whole essay twice: There is no time to write the essay twice.
- To learn new words to use in the essay: The exam is not the time to learn vocabulary.

options.label: A
options.content: To choose relevant points and arrange them in a logical order

options.label: B
options.content: To copy out the question several times

options.label: C
options.content: To write the whole essay twice

options.label: D
options.content: To learn new words to use in the essay

questions.stem: Which is the best way to end an essay?
questions.explanation:
Never just write *In conclusion, as I said…*. A fresh summing-up and a strong final line leave the examiner with a good impression.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Repeat the introduction word for word: Repeating the introduction adds nothing and wastes the last impression.
- Introduce a completely new point: A new point belongs in the body, where it can be developed.
- Write *The End* after the last paragraph: *The End* is not part of an essay's conclusion.

options.label: A
options.content: Repeat the introduction word for word

options.label: B
options.content: Sum up the main idea in fresh words and end with a call to action or a thoughtful final line

options.label: C
options.content: Introduce a completely new point

options.label: D
options.content: Write *The End* after the last paragraph

papers.title: Formal Letter Writing: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on formal letter writing, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A formal letter begins *Dear Sir,*. Which complimentary close is correct?
questions.explanation:
*Yours faithfully,*: capital *Y*, small *f*, a comma. Then the signature and the full name.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Yours sincerely,: As taught in the lessons, *Dear Sir* and *Dear Sir/Madam* take *Yours faithfully*.
- Your's faithfully,: There is no apostrophe in *Yours*.
- Yours Faithfully.  
  *Faithfully* takes a small *f*, and the close ends with a comma, not a full stop.

options.label: A
options.content: Yours sincerely,

options.label: B
options.content: Your's faithfully,

options.label: C
options.content: Yours faithfully,

options.label: D
options.content: Yours Faithfully.

questions.stem: In a formal letter, what comes immediately after the salutation (*Dear Sir,*)?
questions.explanation:
The seven parts in order: writer's address, date, recipient's title and address, salutation, heading, body, and the close with signature and full name.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The recipient's title and address: The recipient's address comes before the salutation.
- The date: The date comes before the salutation, under the writer's address.
- The complimentary close: The close comes at the end, after the body.

options.label: A
options.content: The recipient's title and address

options.label: B
options.content: The date

options.label: C
options.content: The complimentary close

options.label: D
options.content: The heading (title)

questions.stem: A formal letter should end with
questions.explanation:
Add your position in brackets if it matters, for example *(Senior Prefect)*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the writer's first name only: First name only is for informal letters.
- the writer's nickname: A nickname is never used in a formal letter.
- *Your loving friend*: *Your loving friend* is an informal close.

options.label: A
options.content: the complimentary close, the writer's signature and full name

options.label: B
options.content: the writer's first name only

options.label: C
options.content: the writer's nickname

options.label: D
options.content: *Your loving friend*

questions.stem: Which is the best heading for a letter to the Chairman of the city council about rubbish piling up at a market?
questions.explanation:
A good heading tells the reader exactly what the letter is about, in a few words: the problem and the place.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- A LETTER: This does not say what the letter is about.
- RUBBISH: This is too vague: whose rubbish, where, and what is the problem?
- PLEASE HELP US SIR: A heading names the subject; it is not a plea.

options.label: A
options.content: A LETTER

options.label: B
options.content: UNCOLLECTED RUBBISH AT KISSY ROAD MARKET

options.label: C
options.content: RUBBISH

options.label: D
options.content: PLEASE HELP US SIR

questions.stem: Which sentence is written in a suitable formal register?
questions.explanation:
Formal register: complete sentences, standard vocabulary, no slang or contractions, polite and firm.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- You guys need to fix this pipe quick.  
  *You guys* and *quick* are informal, and the tone is disrespectful.
- I'm begging you pls fix it.  
  Contractions, text spellings and begging are not formal register.
- Fix the pipe now or else!  
  A threat is rude; a formal letter is polite but firm.

options.label: A
options.content: You guys need to fix this pipe quick.

options.label: B
options.content: I'm begging you pls fix it.

options.label: C
options.content: I would be grateful if the burst pipe could be repaired promptly.

options.label: D
options.content: Fix the pipe now or else!

questions.stem: Which is the best way to write the date in a formal letter?
questions.explanation:
Write the day, the month in words and the full year, as taught in the lessons.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 14/3/26: Figures alone can be misread: in some countries this would mean the 3rd of a month.
- Thursday: A day of the week is not a date.
- March 2026: The day of the month is missing.

options.label: B
options.content: Thursday

options.label: C
options.content: March 2026

options.label: D
options.content: 14th March, 2026.

questions.stem: Which is the most effective first sentence for a letter of complaint?
questions.explanation:
A formal letter states its purpose at once: what the problem is, where, and for how long.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- How are you and your family?  
  Greetings like this belong in an informal letter.
- I hope this letter meets you in good health.  
  This wastes the opening and says nothing about the complaint.
- My name is Musa and I am in Form Five.  
  The reader needs the purpose first, not personal details.

options.label: A
options.content: I am writing to complain about the irregular supply of electricity to Lumley, which has now continued for a month.

options.label: B
options.content: How are you and your family?

options.label: C
options.content: I hope this letter meets you in good health.

options.label: D
options.content: My name is Musa and I am in Form Five.

papers.title: Informal Letter Writing: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on informal letter writing, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following should NOT appear in an informal letter to a friend?
questions.explanation:
Adding the recipient's address and a heading borrows the formal layout, and it costs organisation marks.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The writer's address and the date: These do appear, at the top right, as in a formal letter.
- A salutation such as *Dear Kadie,*: An informal letter needs a salutation.
- A close such as *Your loving friend,*: An informal letter needs a close.

options.label: A
options.content: The writer's address and the date

options.label: B
options.content: The friend's address and a heading

options.label: C
options.content: A salutation such as *Dear Kadie,*

options.label: D
options.content: A close such as *Your loving friend,*

questions.stem: An informal letter to your cousin should be signed with
questions.explanation:
Close warmly (*Your loving cousin,*) and sign with your first name.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- your full name and position: Full name and position belong in a formal letter.
- a signature and your full name: A signature with the full name is the formal ending.
- your surname only: A surname alone sounds cold and formal to a relative.

options.label: A
options.content: your full name and position

options.label: B
options.content: a signature and your full name

options.label: C
options.content: your first name only

options.label: D
options.content: your surname only

questions.stem: Which salutation is correct for a letter to a close friend called Kadie?
questions.explanation:
An informal salutation has a capital *D*, the person's name and a comma.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Dear Friend,: *Dear Friend* alone is never used; name the friend.
- Dear Sir,: *Dear Sir* is for a formal letter.
- Hello Kadie!!!  
  This is a text message greeting, not a letter salutation.

options.label: A
options.content: Dear Friend,

options.label: B
options.content: Dear Sir,

options.label: C
options.content: Hello Kadie!!!

options.label: D
options.content: Dear Kadie,

questions.stem: Which is the best opening paragraph for an informal letter to a friend?
questions.explanation:
Greet briefly and warmly, then move quickly to the purpose of the letter.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- How are you? How is your mother? How is your father? How is your sister? I hope you are all fine. I am fine too.  
  A paragraph of greetings wastes words and earns no content marks.
- I am writing to complain about your failure to reply to my letters.  
  This is the tone of a formal complaint, not a friendly letter.
- Dear Sir, I hope this letter finds you well.  
  *Dear Sir* is a formal salutation, and the sentence is too stiff.

options.label: A
options.content: It was lovely to get your letter last week. I'm writing to tell you about the new science laboratory at our school.

options.label: B
options.content: How are you? How is your mother? How is your father? How is your sister? I hope you are all fine. I am fine too.

options.label: C
options.content: I am writing to complain about your failure to reply to my letters.

options.label: D
options.content: Dear Sir, I hope this letter finds you well.

questions.stem: A letter to your uncle, an older relative you respect, is best written in
questions.explanation:
Semi-formal letters go to older people you know: uncles, aunts, teachers. The tone is warm but respectful, with fewer contractions and no slang.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- slang and text-message spellings: Slang is wrong in any examination letter, and especially to an older relative.
- the formal layout, with his address and a heading: A letter to a relative does not use the formal layout.
- a stiff formal register ending *Yours faithfully*: *Yours faithfully* is for formal letters to officials.

options.label: A
options.content: slang and text-message spellings

options.label: B
options.content: a warm but respectful semi-formal register

options.label: C
options.content: the formal layout, with his address and a heading

options.label: D
options.content: a stiff formal register ending *Yours faithfully*

questions.stem: Which sentence is acceptable in an informal letter?
questions.explanation:
An informal letter is relaxed and chatty, but it is still marked for correct English.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Me and Amie went to the beach on Saturday.  
  *Me* cannot be the subject of a verb: write *Amie and I*.
- hw r u? hope u ar fyn: Text spellings are never acceptable in an examination letter.
- It was sweet die!  
  Slang like this is not standard English.

options.label: A
options.content: Me and Amie went to the beach on Saturday.

options.label: B
options.content: hw r u? hope u ar fyn

options.label: C
options.content: Amie and I went to the beach on Saturday.

options.label: D
options.content: It was sweet die!

questions.stem: The main part of an informal letter should
questions.explanation:
If the question asks you to tell a friend about changes at your school, the body should describe those changes, one in each paragraph, with details.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- consist mostly of greetings to the family: Greetings earn no content marks.
- be one long paragraph: One long paragraph loses organisation marks.
- copy out the question: Copying the question earns nothing.

options.label: A
options.content: consist mostly of greetings to the family

options.label: B
options.content: be one long paragraph

options.label: C
options.content: copy out the question

options.label: D
options.content: deal fully with what the question asks, in developed paragraphs

papers.title: Speech Writing: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on speech writing, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which is the correct way to begin a speech at a school speech day?
questions.explanation:
The vocative addresses the audience in order of importance, ending with the main body of listeners.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Dear audience,: A speech is not a letter, so it does not begin with *Dear*.
- Fellow students, the Principal, the Chairman,: The vocative follows the order of importance in the hall, so the Chairman comes first.
- Hello everybody!  
  This is too casual and does not recognise the important guests.

options.label: A
options.content: The Chairman, the Principal, members of staff, parents, fellow students,

options.label: B
options.content: Dear audience,

options.label: C
options.content: Fellow students, the Principal, the Chairman,

options.label: D
options.content: Hello everybody!

questions.stem: A speech usually ends with the words
questions.explanation:
Sum up in a fresh way, call the audience to action, then thank them for listening (or for their kind attention).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Yours faithfully,: *Yours faithfully* ends a formal letter.
- The End.  
  *The End* is not used to close a speech.
- Your loving friend,: This closes an informal letter.

options.label: A
options.content: Yours faithfully,

options.label: B
options.content: Thank you for listening.

options.label: C
options.content: The End.

options.label: D
options.content: Your loving friend,

questions.stem: *How many of us slept before midnight last night?* A speaker who asks this, without expecting an answer, is using
questions.explanation:
A rhetorical question makes the audience think about the point, and draws them in.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a signpost: A signpost guides listeners through the points: *My first point… Secondly…*
- the rule of three: The rule of three groups ideas in threes.
- a vocative: The vocative is the opening address to the audience.

options.label: A
options.content: a signpost

options.label: B
options.content: the rule of three

options.label: C
options.content: a rhetorical question

options.label: D
options.content: a vocative

questions.stem: *It steals our time, our sleep and our grades.* This sentence uses
questions.explanation:
Grouping ideas in threes creates a rhythm that is easy to remember: a technique of spoken English.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a rhetorical question: The sentence is a statement, not a question.
- a vocative: It is not an address to the audience.
- a signpost: It does not mark the order of the points.

options.label: A
options.content: a rhetorical question

options.label: B
options.content: a vocative

options.label: C
options.content: a signpost

options.label: D
options.content: the rule of three

questions.stem: Phrases such as *My first point…*, *Secondly…* and *Finally…* are especially useful in a speech because
questions.explanation:
A speech is written to be heard. Clear signposts tell the audience where they are in the argument.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- they make the speech longer: Length is not the purpose; clarity is.
- they replace the vocative: Signposts organise the body; the vocative is still needed at the start.
- examiners count the number of phrases: Examiners mark organisation, not a count of phrases.

options.label: A
options.content: listeners cannot reread, so signposts help them follow

options.label: B
options.content: they make the speech longer

options.label: C
options.content: they replace the vocative

options.label: D
options.content: examiners count the number of phrases

questions.stem: Which opening address suits a debate?
questions.explanation:
Recognise everyone with a role in the debate: the chairman, the judges, the time-keeper and the other speakers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The Paramount Chief, elders, the Councillor, ladies and gentlemen,: This suits a community meeting, not a debate.
- Dear judges,: A debate speech is not a letter.
- My dear friends and family,: This is too informal, and it ignores the chairman and judges.

options.label: A
options.content: The Paramount Chief, elders, the Councillor, ladies and gentlemen,

options.label: B
options.content: The Chairman, panel of judges, the time-keeper, co-debaters, ladies and gentlemen,

options.label: C
options.content: Dear judges,

options.label: D
options.content: My dear friends and family,

questions.stem: After the vocative, a speaker should
questions.explanation:
For example: *I am Fatmata Koroma, the Senior Prefect, and I stand before you to speak on…*

**Why the other options are wrong**

- close with *Thank you for listening*: That belongs at the end of the speech.
- go straight to the final point: The audience needs to know who is speaking and on what topic.
- write *Yours faithfully*: That is a letter close.

options.label: A
options.content: close with *Thank you for listening*

options.label: B
options.content: go straight to the final point

options.label: C
options.content: introduce themselves and state the topic

options.label: D
options.content: write *Yours faithfully*

papers.title: Narrative Essays: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on narrative essays, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In a narrative essay, the climax is
questions.explanation:
A good story builds through rising action to one strong climax, then resolves.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the opening, which sets the scene: The opening introduces who, where and when.
- the lesson learnt at the end: The lesson comes in the reflection, after the climax.
- the title of the story: The title names the story; the climax is a moment inside it.

options.label: A
options.content: the opening, which sets the scene

options.label: B
options.content: the lesson learnt at the end

options.label: C
options.content: the title of the story

options.label: D
options.content: the most tense or important moment of the story

questions.stem: A question says: *Write a story that ends with: "…and that was the last time I ever trusted a stranger."* The candidate should
questions.explanation:
Plan backwards: decide what happened that would make someone say these words, then lead up to them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- begin the story with the given words: The words must end the story, not begin it.
- change the words to fit the story: The given ending must be copied exactly.
- write an essay about strangers in general: The question asks for a story, not a discussion.

options.label: A
options.content: build the story so that the given words are its natural last line, copied exactly

options.label: B
options.content: begin the story with the given words

options.label: C
options.content: change the words to fit the story

options.label: D
options.content: write an essay about strangers in general

questions.stem: For the question *Narrate an experience that taught you a lesson*, the most natural point of view is
questions.explanation:
*I* makes a personal experience immediate, and makes the lesson at the end your own.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the second person (*you*): The second person is rarely used for a personal experience.
- the third person (*he*, *she*): The third person suits a story illustrating a proverb more than a personal experience.
- a mixture of all three: Changing point of view confuses the reader.

options.label: A
options.content: the second person (*you*)

options.label: B
options.content: the first person (*I*)

options.label: C
options.content: the third person (*he*, *she*)

options.label: D
options.content: a mixture of all three

questions.stem: A question says: *Write a story to illustrate the saying "All that glitters is not gold."* The story must
questions.explanation:
For example, something that looks valuable or attractive turns out to be worthless or harmful.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- explain the meaning of each word in the saying: That is an explanation, not a story.
- mention the saying but tell any story at all: Mentioning it is not enough; the events must illustrate it.
- argue whether the saying is true: Arguing belongs in an argumentative essay.

options.label: A
options.content: explain the meaning of each word in the saying

options.label: B
options.content: mention the saying but tell any story at all

options.label: C
options.content: show the meaning of the saying through what happens in it

options.label: D
options.content: argue whether the saying is true

questions.stem: Which sentence best shows, rather than tells, that a character was afraid?
questions.explanation:
Showing lets the reader see the fear in actions and body language, which earns expression marks.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- She was very afraid.  
  This tells the reader the feeling instead of showing it.
- She was afraid because she was scared.  
  This repeats the same idea and shows nothing.
- Fear is a feeling everybody has.  
  This is a general statement, not part of the story.

options.label: A
options.content: She was very afraid.

options.label: B
options.content: She was afraid because she was scared.

options.label: C
options.content: Fear is a feeling everybody has.

options.label: D
options.content: Her hands shook as she reached for the door, and she held her breath.

questions.stem: *I woke up. I bathed. I went to school. We had Maths. Then we had lunch.* What is the main weakness of this opening to a story?
questions.explanation:
Start close to the action and build towards one important moment.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- It is written in the past tense: The past tense is normal for a narrative.
- It is written in the first person: The first person is a good choice for many stories.
- Its sentences are ungrammatical: Each sentence is correct; the problem is the dull, list-like structure.

options.label: A
options.content: It lists events like a diary, with no build-up towards a climax

options.label: B
options.content: It is written in the past tense

options.label: C
options.content: It is written in the first person

options.label: D
options.content: Its sentences are ungrammatical

questions.stem: How much dialogue should a narrative essay contain?
questions.explanation:
Use dialogue sparingly, set out correctly, where it reveals character or raises tension.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- None at all: A few lines of dialogue can bring a key moment to life.
- Most of the story: A story that is mostly conversation loses the description that earns marks.
- Only in the title: Dialogue belongs in the story, not the title.

options.label: A
options.content: None at all

options.label: B
options.content: A little, for key moments

options.label: C
options.content: Most of the story

options.label: D
options.content: Only in the title

papers.title: Descriptive Essays: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on descriptive essays, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the senses most effectively in a description of a market?
questions.explanation:
Smell, sound and touch make the reader feel present; a good description uses several senses.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The market is very big and there are many people.  
  This is vague and uses no senses.
- They sell many things like rice, oil, clothes, shoes and phones.  
  A list of items is not a description.
- The market is nice and I like it.  
  *Nice* says nothing the reader can see, hear or smell.

options.label: A
options.content: The market is very big and there are many people.

options.label: B
options.content: They sell many things like rice, oil, clothes, shoes and phones.

options.label: C
options.content: The smell of smoked fish mixed with the blare of a trader's radio and the heat rising from the zinc roofs.

options.label: D
options.content: The market is nice and I like it.

questions.stem: The 'dominant impression' of a descriptive essay is
questions.explanation:
For example, a market described as *the heartbeat of the town*: every detail supports that impression.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the first sentence of the essay: The dominant impression runs through the whole essay, though it is often stated early.
- a list of everything the writer saw: A list has no overall impression.
- the writer's name under the title: The writer's name is part of the format of an article.

options.label: A
options.content: the first sentence of the essay

options.label: B
options.content: a list of everything the writer saw

options.label: C
options.content: the writer's name under the title

options.label: D
options.content: the single overall feeling or idea that the description builds up

questions.stem: Which is the best way to organise a description of a place?
questions.explanation:
A route lets the reader move through the place with the writer.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- List the things in alphabetical order: Alphabetical order has nothing to do with how a place is experienced.
- Jump from detail to detail at random: Random details confuse the reader.
- Describe only the weather: The weather is only one small part of a place.

options.label: A
options.content: Follow a route through space or time, such as from the entrance to the centre

options.label: B
options.content: List the things in alphabetical order

options.label: C
options.content: Jump from detail to detail at random

options.label: D
options.content: Describe only the weather

questions.stem: When describing a person, a good order is
questions.explanation:
Begin with what is seen, then reveal character through habits, speech and actions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- from the person's date of birth to the present day: That is a biography, not a description.
- from the weather on the day you met to the person's name: The weather is not the subject.
- only their clothes, with nothing about character: Clothes alone do not bring a person to life.

options.label: A
options.content: from the person's date of birth to the present day

options.label: B
options.content: from outward appearance to inner character and habits

options.label: C
options.content: from the weather on the day you met to the person's name

options.label: D
options.content: only their clothes, with nothing about character

questions.stem: Which word most vividly replaces *walked* in *The tired old man walked slowly up the hill*?
questions.explanation:
*Trudged* means walked slowly and heavily, as if tired: one precise word paints the picture.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- went: *Went* is even more general than *walked*.
- moved: *Moved* is vague and adds no picture.
- sprinted: *Sprinted* means ran fast, which contradicts *tired* and *slowly*.

options.label: A
options.content: went

options.label: B
options.content: moved

options.label: C
options.content: trudged

options.label: D
options.content: sprinted

questions.stem: Figurative language, such as similes and metaphors, in a descriptive essay should be
questions.explanation:
One fresh, accurate image is worth more than many stale ones.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- avoided completely: A well-chosen image strengthens a description.
- used in every sentence to impress the examiner: Overloading every sentence with images makes the writing heavy and unclear.
- copied from a list of memorised expressions: Memorised images rarely fit the scene being described.

options.label: A
options.content: avoided completely

options.label: B
options.content: used in every sentence to impress the examiner

options.label: C
options.content: copied from a list of memorised expressions

options.label: D
options.content: used where it adds a clear picture, not crowded into every sentence

questions.stem: A question asks you to describe an Independence Day celebration in your town. Which organisation suits it best?
questions.explanation:
Organise a place by a route, a person from outside to inside, and an event in time order.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Alphabetical order of the people present: Alphabetical order does not follow the event.
- The most boring parts first: Order the event so that the reader follows it naturally.
- One long paragraph with no order: One unordered paragraph loses organisation marks.

options.label: A
options.content: Time order, from the start of the day to the end

options.label: B
options.content: Alphabetical order of the people present

options.label: C
options.content: The most boring parts first

options.label: D
options.content: One long paragraph with no order

papers.title: Argumentative Essays: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on argumentative essays, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In an argumentative essay, the introduction should
questions.explanation:
A clear thesis tells the examiner what the whole essay will prove.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- avoid taking any side: An argumentative essay must take a side.
- set out every argument in full: The arguments are developed in the body paragraphs.
- end with *Thank you for listening*: That closes a speech, not an essay introduction.

options.label: A
options.content: avoid taking any side

options.label: B
options.content: state the writer's position clearly

options.label: C
options.content: set out every argument in full

options.label: D
options.content: end with *Thank you for listening*

questions.stem: Asked *Should students be allowed phones in school?*, a candidate writes: *Phones have advantages and disadvantages, so it depends.* The main weakness is that
questions.explanation:
You may admit the other side has points, but you must decide and argue for one position.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the essay mentions phones: The topic is phones, so mentioning them is necessary.
- the essay is written in English: There is nothing wrong with the language choice.
- the sentence is too short: Length is not the main problem; sitting on the fence is.

options.label: A
options.content: the essay mentions phones

options.label: B
options.content: the essay is written in English

options.label: C
options.content: the essay does not take a clear position

options.label: D
options.content: the sentence is too short

questions.stem: Why should a strong argumentative essay mention the best argument on the other side?
questions.explanation:
The counter-argument and rebuttal show the examiner that you have thought about both sides and can defend your view.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- To change sides at the end of the essay: Changing sides makes the essay contradict itself.
- To fill up space: Every paragraph should do real work.
- To show that the writer is unsure: A rebuttal shows confidence, not doubt.

options.label: A
options.content: To change sides at the end of the essay

options.label: B
options.content: To fill up space

options.label: C
options.content: To show that the writer is unsure

options.label: D
options.content: To answer it fairly and show why the writer's position is still stronger

questions.stem: In the PEEL method for argument paragraphs, the letters stand for
questions.explanation:
Make the point, support it with evidence, explain why it matters, and link to the next point.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Paragraph, Essay, Example, Language: These are not the steps of the method.
- Point, Emotion, Ending, Letter: Emotion, ending and letter are not steps of the method.
- Purpose, Evidence, Expression, List: This mixes up marking areas with paragraph steps.

options.label: A
options.content: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link

options.label: B
options.content: Paragraph, Essay, Example, Language

options.label: C
options.content: Point, Emotion, Ending, Letter

options.label: D
options.content: Purpose, Evidence, Expression, List

questions.stem: Which is the best kind of evidence for a WASSCE argumentative essay?
questions.explanation:
Good evidence includes examples, well-known facts, cause-and-effect reasoning and comparisons.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Precise statistics that you invent: Invented statistics are not evidence, and examiners can tell.
- Insults to people who disagree: Insults weaken an argument and lose marks.
- A list of famous names with no explanation: Names without explanation do not support a point.

options.label: A
options.content: Precise statistics that you invent

options.label: B
options.content: Examples from your community and facts that are widely known

options.label: C
options.content: Insults to people who disagree

options.label: D
options.content: A list of famous names with no explanation

questions.stem: Which sentence states a clear position for an essay on boarding schools?
questions.explanation:
A position states what the writer believes and, often, what should be done.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Some people like boarding schools and some do not.  
  This describes opinions without taking a position.
- Boarding schools are a topic that many people talk about.  
  This says nothing about the writer's view.
- This essay will look at boarding schools.  
  This announces the topic but not a position.

options.label: A
options.content: Some people like boarding schools and some do not.

options.label: B
options.content: Boarding schools are a topic that many people talk about.

options.label: C
options.content: Boarding schools give students the best chance to succeed, and the government should build more of them.

options.label: D
options.content: This essay will look at boarding schools.

questions.stem: The conclusion of an argumentative essay should
questions.explanation:
A strong conclusion leaves the reader persuaded and clear about what should happen next.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- introduce a new argument: New arguments belong in the body, where they can be developed.
- switch to the opposite side: Switching sides undoes the whole essay.
- copy the introduction word for word: Repeating the introduction adds nothing.

options.label: A
options.content: introduce a new argument

options.label: B
options.content: switch to the opposite side

options.label: C
options.content: copy the introduction word for word

options.label: D
options.content: restate the position in fresh words and end with a call to action or a striking thought

papers.title: Report Writing: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on report writing, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which part of a report states who asked for it, its purpose and how the information was gathered?
questions.explanation:
Report format: title, introduction, findings, recommendations, conclusion, and a signature block with name, position and date.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The findings: The findings set out what was found.
- The recommendations: The recommendations suggest what should be done.
- The conclusion: The conclusion is a brief closing statement.

options.label: A
options.content: The introduction

options.label: B
options.content: The findings

options.label: C
options.content: The recommendations

options.label: D
options.content: The conclusion

questions.stem: Which sentence is written in the style of a formal report?
questions.explanation:
Reports are objective: they state what was observed, with numbers where possible.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The toilets were absolutely disgusting!  
  A report gives facts, not feelings or exclamations.
- The smell nearly killed me!  
  This is an exaggerated personal reaction, not an objective finding.
- I think the toilets are bad, maybe.  
  A report is definite and factual, not vague.

options.label: A
options.content: The toilets were absolutely disgusting!

options.label: B
options.content: Four of the six toilets were out of use at the time of the inspection.

options.label: C
options.content: The smell nearly killed me!

options.label: D
options.content: I think the toilets are bad, maybe.

questions.stem: Recommendations in a report are usually written with *should*. Which is a well-written recommendation?
questions.explanation:
A recommendation is a practical step that someone can carry out.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- I wish someone would repair the tank.  
  A wish is not a recommendation.
- Repair the tank now!  
  A command in capitals and exclamations is not the style of a report.
- Why has nobody repaired the tank?  
  A question is not a recommendation.

options.label: A
options.content: I wish someone would repair the tank.

options.label: B
options.content: Repair the tank now!

options.label: C
options.content: The water tank should be repaired as a matter of urgency.

options.label: D
options.content: Why has nobody repaired the tank?

questions.stem: Reports often use the passive voice, as in *The toilets were inspected on Monday.* This is because
questions.explanation:
The passive keeps attention on the facts, which suits an objective report.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the passive voice is always shorter: The passive is often longer, not shorter.
- the active voice is grammatically wrong: The active voice is correct; the passive simply suits reports.
- reports must not contain any verbs: Reports contain verbs like any other writing.

options.label: A
options.content: the passive voice is always shorter

options.label: B
options.content: the active voice is grammatically wrong

options.label: C
options.content: reports must not contain any verbs

options.label: D
options.content: what was done matters more than who did it

questions.stem: In a report, what the committee observed during its visit is normally written in
questions.explanation:
Past tense for what was found (*The committee visited…*); present tense for the situation now (*The tank is empty…*).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the future tense: The future tense is for what will happen, not what was found.
- the imperative mood: The imperative gives commands.
- a mixture of tenses in each sentence: Mixing tenses confuses the reader.

options.label: A
options.content: the past tense

options.label: B
options.content: the future tense

options.label: C
options.content: the imperative mood

options.label: D
options.content: a mixture of tenses in each sentence

questions.stem: A report ends with
questions.explanation:
For example: *Musa Bangura (Secretary, Health Club), 12th March, 2026.*

**Why the other options are wrong**

- *Yours faithfully,*: That is the close of a formal letter.
- *Thank you for listening.*: That closes a speech.
- *The End*: A report does not end with *The End*.

options.label: A
options.content: *Yours faithfully,*

options.label: B
options.content: the writer's name, position and the date

options.label: C
options.content: *Thank you for listening.*

options.label: D
options.content: *The End*

questions.stem: A report on sanitation begins: *It was a bright sunny morning and we were all excited as we set out.* What is wrong with this opening?
questions.explanation:
A report opens with its purpose and how the information was gathered, in a factual style.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- It uses the past tense: The past tense is correct for what was done.
- It mentions the morning: Mentioning the time is not the fault; the story-telling style is.
- It is too short: Its length is not the problem.

options.label: A
options.content: It uses the past tense

options.label: B
options.content: It mentions the morning

options.label: C
options.content: It reads like a story instead of stating the report's purpose

options.label: D
options.content: It is too short

papers.title: Article Writing: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on article writing, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: An article for a school magazine should have
questions.explanation:
The writer's name may go below the title as a by-line or at the end.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the writer's address, the date and *Dear Editor,*: These belong to a letter to the editor.
- a vocative such as *The Principal, fellow students,*: A vocative begins a speech.
- *Yours faithfully* and a signature: These close a formal letter.

options.label: A
options.content: the writer's address, the date and *Dear Editor,*

options.label: B
options.content: a vocative such as *The Principal, fellow students,*

options.label: C
options.content: *Yours faithfully* and a signature

options.label: D
options.content: a title and the writer's name, but no salutation or complimentary close

questions.stem: A candidate asked to write an article begins with *Dear Editor,* and ends with *Yours faithfully*. The candidate has
questions.explanation:
Read the question carefully: an *article* and a *letter to the editor* have different formats, and the wrong one costs organisation marks.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- written a perfect article: An article has no salutation and no close.
- written a speech: A speech begins with a vocative and ends with *Thank you for listening*.
- written a report: A report has a title, introduction, findings and recommendations.

options.label: A
options.content: written a letter to the editor instead of an article

options.label: B
options.content: written a perfect article

options.label: C
options.content: written a speech

options.label: D
options.content: written a report

questions.stem: Which is the best opening for an article on reading for pleasure?
questions.explanation:
A hook, such as a question to the reader, a striking fact or a short scene, makes the reader want to go on.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- I am writing to inform you that reading is good.  
  *I am writing to inform you* is the language of a letter, and the sentence is flat.
- Reading. Reading is reading.  
  This says nothing and does not hook the reader.
- Dear Sir, reading is important.  
  An article does not begin with a salutation.

options.label: A
options.content: I am writing to inform you that reading is good.

options.label: B
options.content: When did you last read a book that nobody made you read?

options.label: C
options.content: Reading. Reading is reading.

options.label: D
options.content: Dear Sir, reading is important.

questions.stem: An article for a school magazine should be written in a tone that is
questions.explanation:
Match the tone to the readers: friendly for a school magazine, serious but readable for a national newspaper.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- full of slang and text spellings: Slang and text spellings are never acceptable in the examination.
- as stiff as a legal document: A stiff tone loses the young readers of a magazine.
- angry and insulting: An insulting tone turns readers against the writer.

options.label: A
options.content: full of slang and text spellings

options.label: B
options.content: as stiff as a legal document

options.label: C
options.content: lively and friendly, but correct

options.label: D
options.content: angry and insulting

questions.stem: Which is the most effective title for an article on preventing floods in Freetown?
questions.explanation:
A good title is short, specific and catches the reader's eye.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ARTICLE: This does not say what the article is about.
- FLOOD: This is vague and says nothing about prevention.
- MY ARTICLE ON THE TOPIC GIVEN: This is not a real title.

options.label: A
options.content: ARTICLE

options.label: B
options.content: FLOOD

options.label: C
options.content: MY ARTICLE ON THE TOPIC GIVEN

options.label: D
options.content: CLEAR THE DRAINS, SAVE THE CITY

questions.stem: In an article, the writer's name may be placed
questions.explanation:
For example: *By Fatmata Koroma* under the title.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- at the top right, with the writer's address: An article has no address.
- after *Yours faithfully*: An article has no complimentary close.
- nowhere: articles never show the writer's name: The writer's name is part of the format.

options.label: A
options.content: below the title as a by-line, or at the end

options.label: B
options.content: at the top right, with the writer's address

options.label: C
options.content: after *Yours faithfully*

options.label: D
options.content: nowhere: articles never show the writer's name

questions.stem: An article on drug abuse among young people is best ended with
questions.explanation:
End by telling readers what they can do, and leave them with a strong final line.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a new cause of drug abuse not mentioned before: New points belong in the body.
- *Yours faithfully* and the writer's signature: That is the close of a formal letter.
- the same words as the title: Repeating the title adds nothing.

options.label: A
options.content: a new cause of drug abuse not mentioned before

options.label: B
options.content: practical steps and a call to action

options.label: C
options.content: *Yours faithfully* and the writer's signature

options.label: D
options.content: the same words as the title

papers.title: Expository Essays: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on expository essays, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: An expository essay mainly
questions.explanation:
Expository questions ask *what*, *how* or *why*: causes and effects, steps in a process, types of something, problems and solutions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- tells a story: Telling a story is narrative writing.
- describes a scene through the senses: That is descriptive writing.
- persuades the reader to accept a view: Persuading is argumentative writing.

options.label: A
options.content: tells a story

options.label: B
options.content: describes a scene through the senses

options.label: C
options.content: explains or informs, without arguing for a side

options.label: D
options.content: persuades the reader to accept a view

questions.stem: How should an essay on *the steps involved in making gari* be organised?
questions.explanation:
Process essays use sequence words: *first*, *next*, *then*, *after that*, *finally*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- From the most interesting step to the least: A process must follow the order in which it is done.
- In alphabetical order of the tools used: Alphabetical order would mix up the process.
- As an argument for eating gari: The question asks for steps, not an argument.

options.label: A
options.content: From the most interesting step to the least

options.label: B
options.content: In alphabetical order of the tools used

options.label: C
options.content: As an argument for eating gari

options.label: D
options.content: In time order, one step after another

questions.stem: Which transition word introduces an effect or result?
questions.explanation:
Effect: as a result, therefore, consequently, so. Cause: because, since, due to, owing to.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- because: *Because* introduces a cause.
- for example: *For example* introduces an example.
- however: *However* introduces a contrast.

options.label: A
options.content: consequently

options.label: B
options.content: because

options.label: C
options.content: for example

options.label: D
options.content: however

questions.stem: Asked to *explain the causes of rural–urban migration in Sierra Leone*, a candidate spends half the essay arguing that migration is bad. What is the weakness?
questions.explanation:
Answer the question set: explain the causes fully, each in its own paragraph.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The essay mentions Sierra Leone: The question asks about Sierra Leone.
- The essay uses examples: Examples are a strength of an expository essay.
- The essay is too well organised: Good organisation is never a weakness.

options.label: A
options.content: The essay mentions Sierra Leone

options.label: B
options.content: The question asks for an explanation, not an argument

options.label: C
options.content: The essay uses examples

options.label: D
options.content: The essay is too well organised

questions.stem: A question asks *What are the types of pollution?* The clearest plan is
questions.explanation:
Classification essays treat each type in turn, with its features.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- all the types mixed together in one paragraph: Mixing types together is confusing and loses organisation marks.
- a story about a polluted river: The question asks for an explanation of types, not a story.
- an argument that pollution should be banned: The question does not ask for an argument.

options.label: A
options.content: all the types mixed together in one paragraph

options.label: B
options.content: a story about a polluted river

options.label: C
options.content: one type per paragraph, with its features and examples

options.label: D
options.content: an argument that pollution should be banned

questions.stem: In an expository essay, a key term such as *deforestation* should be
questions.explanation:
For example: *Deforestation, the clearing of forest land for farming, timber or building, …*

**Why the other options are wrong**

- never defined, because examiners already know it: Defining terms shows understanding and makes the essay clear.
- defined only in the conclusion: By the conclusion the reader has already needed the definition.
- replaced by a word the writer invents: Invented words confuse the reader.

options.label: A
options.content: never defined, because examiners already know it

options.label: B
options.content: defined only in the conclusion

options.label: C
options.content: replaced by a word the writer invents

options.label: D
options.content: defined clearly the first time it is used

questions.stem: For the question *What are the causes and effects of examination malpractice?*, a clear plan is
questions.explanation:
Alternatively, take one cause and its effects at a time; either way, the order must be clear and both parts answered.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the effects only: The causes are part of the question too.
- causes and effects mixed at random: Random order makes the logic hard to follow.
- one paragraph for the whole essay: Each point needs its own developed paragraph.

options.label: A
options.content: the causes first, then the effects

options.label: B
options.content: the effects only

options.label: C
options.content: causes and effects mixed at random

options.label: D
options.content: one paragraph for the whole essay

papers.title: Creative Writing: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on creative writing, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Why should a candidate avoid ending a story with *I woke up and it was all a dream*?
questions.explanation:
Clichés such as *Once upon a time* and the dream ending tell the examiner you have not tried. Find a fresh ending.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Dreams are not allowed in examination stories: Dreams are allowed; the problem is the overused ending.
- It is grammatically incorrect: The sentence is grammatical; the problem is the cliché.
- It makes the story too long: Length is not the problem.

options.label: A
options.content: Dreams are not allowed in examination stories

options.label: B
options.content: It is a tired cliché that cancels everything the story built up

options.label: C
options.content: It is grammatically incorrect

options.label: D
options.content: It makes the story too long

questions.stem: In a story of about 500 words, the best plan is to
questions.explanation:
One idea, done well, leaves room for detail, tension and a satisfying ending.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- tell the whole of a character's life: A whole life cannot be told well in 500 words.
- include as many events as possible: Too many events leave no room to develop any of them.
- describe every character in the village: Too many characters crowd the story.

options.label: A
options.content: tell the whole of a character's life

options.label: B
options.content: include as many events as possible

options.label: C
options.content: build the story around one moment, one change or one surprise

options.label: D
options.content: describe every character in the village

questions.stem: Short sentences such as *The door opened. Nobody was there.* are used in a story to
questions.explanation:
Varying sentence length controls pace: short for action and suspense, longer for description.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- slow the story down for reflection: Longer sentences slow the pace for reflection and description.
- show the writer's knowledge of grammar: Sentence length is chosen for effect, not to display grammar.
- fill up the required number of words: Short sentences add few words; they are used for effect.

options.label: A
options.content: slow the story down for reflection

options.label: B
options.content: show the writer's knowledge of grammar

options.label: C
options.content: fill up the required number of words

options.label: D
options.content: speed up the pace and build tension

questions.stem: A question says: *Write a story beginning: "The letter had been hidden under the mat for ten years."* The candidate should
questions.explanation:
Then answer the questions the sentence raises: who hid the letter, why, and what happens when it is found.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- end the story with the given sentence: The sentence must begin the story, not end it.
- change the sentence to make it more interesting: The given opening must be copied exactly.
- write a letter instead of a story: The question asks for a story about a letter, not a letter.

options.label: A
options.content: begin with the given sentence exactly as written

options.label: B
options.content: end the story with the given sentence

options.label: C
options.content: change the sentence to make it more interesting

options.label: D
options.content: write a letter instead of a story

questions.stem: A twist at the end of a story
questions.explanation:
A good twist surprises, but it makes sense when the reader thinks back over the clues.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- repeats the opening sentence: Repeating the opening is not a twist.
- introduces a new character in the last line with no meaning: A random new character confuses rather than surprises.
- tells the reader that the story was a dream: The dream ending is a cliché, not a twist.

options.label: A
options.content: repeats the opening sentence

options.label: B
options.content: reveals something that changes how the reader sees the whole story

options.label: C
options.content: introduces a new character in the last line with no meaning

options.label: D
options.content: tells the reader that the story was a dream

questions.stem: Telling a story in the third person (*he*, *she*, *they*) gives the writer
questions.explanation:
First person is intimate and immediate; third person can move between characters.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a close view of one mind only: A close view of one mind is the strength of the first person.
- no need to describe anything: Every point of view needs description.
- permission to change point of view in every paragraph: Point of view should stay consistent.

options.label: A
options.content: a close view of one mind only

options.label: B
options.content: no need to describe anything

options.label: C
options.content: more distance and the freedom to show several characters

options.label: D
options.content: permission to change point of view in every paragraph

questions.stem: Which sentence brings a character to life most effectively?
questions.explanation:
One telling habit or detail shows a character in a few strokes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Pa Kamara was a nice old man.  
  *Nice* tells us nothing the reader can picture.
- Pa Kamara was a man who was old and nice and good.  
  A string of vague adjectives does not create a character.
- Pa Kamara was a character in the story.  
  This says nothing about him at all.

options.label: A
options.content: Pa Kamara was a nice old man.

options.label: B
options.content: Pa Kamara was a man who was old and nice and good.

options.label: C
options.content: Pa Kamara was a character in the story.

options.label: D
options.content: Pa Kamara tapped his walking stick twice before every sentence, as if calling the room to order.
